rows.text: Honestly smoother than I expected for a task this heavy. Assembling Module 1 was a guided checklist with a live 0/8 to 8/8 progress counter, the portal generated the administrative leaves (1.0, 1.2.1, 1.2.3, 1.2.4, 1.6) and let me upload the bilingual monograph and labelling — I always knew what was left. The only genuine friction was the export 409, but that was intentional and the fix (file the REP Dossier ID Request, then Rename to the real e478210) was spelled out in the finding itself. Compared to wrangling docuBridge backbones by hand, this was a clean, linear run.

Honestly, easier than I expected for something this regulated. Building Module 1 was a clean checklist with live progress (0/8 climbing to 100%), generate-or-upload per leaf, and the bilingual EN+FR handling on 1.3.1 and 1.3.3 was correct without me fighting it. The only real friction was the placeholder-ID block at export, but that is friction I want — it took one Rename with a reason and a re-validate to clear, maybe two minutes. The lifecycle 0001 replace filed itself as a supersede automatically rather than a duplicate, which is exactly where docuBridge usually makes me think.

Honestly smoother than my usual eCTD Office + GlobalSubmit workflow. The Module 1 checklist drove me straight through all 8 leaves — generate for the admin forms, upload for the bilingual PM and labelling — with a live progress counter so I always knew what was left. The only real work was fixing the placeholder-ID block, and even that was one Rename with a reason. Twenty-plus steps and I never once had to go hunt for what to do next.

Genuinely smooth for what is normally a fiddly, error-prone assembly. Building Module 1 was fast — the generate/upload affordances per section with a live 0/8 to 8/8 progress counter meant I always knew exactly what was left, and the bilingual EN+FR handling on 1.3.1 and 1.3.3 was handled correctly without me fighting the tool. The placeholder-to-real Dossier ID re-key carried all placed content over unchanged, and the 0001 replace was a single upload that auto-resolved to a lifecycle REPLACE. Compared to hand-assembling in eCTD Office, this cut most of the tedium.

Honestly, easier than I expected. The Module 1 checklist showed all 8 required docs with a running percentage, so I always knew what was left — that's a lot friendlier than the Word template folder I usually copy from. Generating the cover letter, application form, attestation, Form V and CS-BE straight from the dossier details saved me the most painful part, and uploads for the bilingual PM and labelling were just drag-in. The only real thinking moments were the placeholder-ID situation and the sequence 0001 replace, but the messages walked me through both.

Honestly easier than I expected for something this involved. The Module 1 checklist told me exactly which 8 documents were needed and ticked up a percentage as I went (12, 25, 38... to 100%), so I never had to guess whether I'd missed a leaf like my seniors always warn me about. Five sections the portal generated for me and three I uploaded; the bilingual EN+FR ones for the Product Monograph and Labelling just worked. The one spot I had to stop and think was the placeholder-ID block, but even that spelled out the fix (file a REP Dossier ID Request, then Rename), so I got unstuck without pinging anyone.

Honestly easier than I expected for something this regulated. The Module 1 checklist walked me through all 8 required leaves with a live progress counter, generate-or-upload on each, and the bilingual EN+FR handling on the monograph and labelling was done for me. The only real friction was the export block, but that turned out to be the system doing its job, not me fumbling — the rename-to-real-Dossier-ID and re-validate flow was two clicks and it cleared.

Honestly easier than I expected for something this regulated. The Module 1 checklist told me exactly which 8 leaves were required, the generate/upload affordances were right there, and the progress bar (0/8 up to 100%) meant I never had to guess whether I'd missed a document. The one place I paused was the placeholder-ID rename step, but the banner up front had already warned me d4821 wasn't real, so re-keying to e478210 with a reason-for-change felt natural rather than alarming. The bilingual EN+FR uploads for 1.3.1 and 1.3.3 were handled cleanly without me hunting for how to attach two files.

Genuinely smooth for someone who knows the backbone. The Module 1 checklist told me exactly what 8 leaves I owed — 1.0, 1.2.1, 1.2.2, 1.2.3, 1.2.4, 1.3.1, 1.3.3, 1.6 — with the bilingual flag on the PM and Labelling, and the progress counter (0/8 up to 8/8) meant I never had to guess whether I'd missed something. Generate-vs-upload was sensibly split (I'd never trust an auto-generated PM, and it correctly forced upload there). The one place I'd stumble is the placeholder-to-real-ID Rename — a first-timer won't know that's the fix until validation spells it out, but it did spell it out.

Honestly smoother than I expected — the Module 1 checklist gave me the 8 required leaves up front with a live 0/8 progress counter, so I never had to cross-check against my own regional backbone list. Generating 1.0, 1.2.1, 1.2.3, 1.2.4 and 1.6 and uploading the fees, PM and labelling was a handful of clicks, and the bilingual sections correctly demanded both EN and FR. Hitting the 409 export block was momentarily jarring, but the fix (Rename to the real Dossier ID, re-validate, re-export) was obvious and quick. The e-sign, attestation, and 0001 replace steps were each a single well-labeled action.

Honestly smoother than I expected for something this regulated. The Module 1 checklist told me exactly what 8 documents I needed, five of them the portal just generated from my company details, and the progress bar ticking 12%, 25%... 100% meant I never had to guess if I was done. The only real work was uploading the bilingual monograph and labelling PDFs, and even the placeholder-ID fix was one Rename with a reason. As a non-regulatory founder, I got through it without my $180k consultant holding my hand.

Honestly smoother than I expected for something this regulated. Generating five of the Module 1 docs from the identifiers I'd already entered meant I wasn't hunting for templates, and the progress bar ticking 12 to 25 to 100 kept me oriented. The e-sign and 0001 replace steps were the only places I slowed down, and even those were just fill-in-the-blank plus a click. As a non-regulatory founder I got through the whole thing without calling my consultant, which is the entire point.

Genuinely smooth for the shape of work I actually do. Module 1 filled leaf by leaf with live progress (0/8 to 100%), generate-vs-upload was correctly gated per section (fees and PM/labelling upload-only, bilingual EN+FR captured properly), and the rename re-key carried all placed content over without me re-placing anything. The only friction is the same as my current tooling: I still have to go get the real Dossier ID out-of-band via REP before I can clear the gate — but the tool is honest that that is external, so that is expected, not a defect.

Honestly smooth for a first run. The Module 1 checklist drove me straight down the eight required leaves, the generate/upload affordances were exactly where I expected, and the placeholder-to-real Rename re-keyed everything without me re-placing a single document. The only real friction — the export 409 and the CA-REP-0001 block — is friction I *want*, and clearing it via Rename then re-validate was two clicks. I got a signed, externally-attested, lifecycle-0001 filing end to end without once reaching for docuBridge.

Honestly smoother than I expected for something this regulated. The Module 1 checklist did the sequencing for me — 8 required leaves, a running percent, generate-or-upload on each — so I never had to guess what was missing or in what order. The one real friction point was the placeholder-to-real Dossier ID, but that's a genuine Health Canada dependency (you can't invent the REP ID), and the tool handled the re-key cleanly with content carried over. As a coordinator who lives in Smartsheet, I could run this without authoring a single document myself.

Honestly easier than I expected for something this regulated. The only real friction points were conceptual, not UI: knowing I had to file a REP Dossier ID Request out-of-band, and knowing that "Rename" was the way to swap the placeholder for the real ID. As a coordinator who doesn't author, I could actually run this whole sequence.

Honestly, easier than I expected. The one place I had to stop and think was the placeholder-ID block, but even that pointed me straight to the fix (file the REP Dossier ID Request, then Rename), so I never felt stuck.

Honestly easier than I expected for something this involved. The module builder walked me down a checklist of 8 documents with a running percentage, so I always knew what was left — I generated the forms I trusted the tool to fill and uploaded my own monograph and labelling PDFs. The lifecycle bits (opening 0001, re-filing the cover letter as a replace) I'd want to do a second time before I felt fluent, but nothing blocked me or left me guessing.

Honestly, easier than I feared. Building Module 1 was just working down a checklist of 8 documents with a progress bar ticking up 12, 25, 38 percent, and I could upload my own PDFs where it mattered, like the bilingual Product Monograph and Labelling. The rename from the placeholder d4821 to the real e478210 carried all my content over without me re-doing anything, which is where a paper-and-Word man like me usually loses a whole afternoon. The e-sign and the 0001 replace were a couple more clicks, not a new ordeal.

Genuinely smooth for someone who files ANDS all day. The Module 1 checklist drove me straight through 8/8 with a clear progress counter, generate-or-upload was obvious per leaf, and the bilingual EN+FR sections behaved. The only real friction was the placeholder-ID block, but that was intentional friction I actually wanted, and the Rename fixed it in one call. I got to a signed, exported, lifecycle-0001 filing without ever guessing what to do next.

Genuinely smooth for a task that is usually a slog. Module 1 filled to 100% in a handful of clicks — generate for the forms, upload for the monograph and labelling with EN+FR handled as one bilingual leaf — and the rename re-keyed my placeholder to e478210 without me re-placing a single document. The only real thought required was resolving CA-REP-0001, which was self-explanatory. Compared to hand-building an index in Freyr, this was faster and I never touched raw XML.

Honestly easier than I feared for someone who has never touched eCTD. The Module 1 checklist told me exactly which 8 documents were required, generated five of them for me, and let me upload the monograph and labelling as bilingual EN/FR pairs, with a running 0/8 to 8/8 progress bar so I always knew where I stood. The one genuine friction point — the placeholder ID blocking export — was the system working as designed, and the Rename step to set the real HC ID e478210 was a single action that carried all my content over. The 0001 replace-a-leaf lifecycle step is where a novice like me would slow down, but the portal filed it as a REPLACE automatically rather than making me understand the mechanics.

Honestly, easier than I feared for someone who's never touched eCTD. The Module 1 checklist gave me all 8 required leaves up front, five of them the portal generated for me from the details I'd already entered, and the two bilingual ones just wanted EN+FR PDFs. The one genuine friction was the placeholder-ID rename step, but the tool told me exactly what to do and it flowed. I got from empty dossier to a signed, exportable, lifecycle-correct sequence in one sitting.

Very clear at nearly every step. The validation report named the exact rule (CA-REP-0001) with a plain-language message and told me the remedy, the export block said "validation_not_passed" and listed the blocking finding instead of dumping a broken zip, and the two-signal validate view kept the structural PASS visually separate from the attested eValidator PASS. What I appreciated most was the honesty labelling — "structural checks only, NOT Health Canada's eValidator" and "USER-ATTESTED external result" — so there was never ambiguity about who verified what.

At every step I knew what the system was telling me. The validation report named the rule (CA-REP-0001) and told me the exact remedy — file a Dossier ID Request through REP, then Rename — not a vague red X. The 409 export block said "validation_not_passed" and echoed the blocking finding instead of handing me a bad zip. And the current-view/outline showing operation='replace' with modified_leaf pointing back at m1-0-1-cover-letter is precisely the relationship an HC reviewer replays, so I could confirm the lifecycle was right.

Very clear at every step. The validation report gave me an actual rule ID (CA-REP-0001) with a plain-language fix — file a Dossier ID Request through REP, then Rename — which is exactly how I think about it. The export block said validation_not_passed and named the blocking finding instead of handing me a broken zip, and the lifecycle view spelled out operation=replace with a back-pointer to the superseded 0000 leaf. I was never guessing what the system meant.

At every step I knew what the system was telling me. The validation report named the exact rule (CA-REP-0001) with a plain-language message AND the remediation ("file a Dossier ID Request through REP, then Rename"), which is exactly how I think. The 409 export block didn't just fail — it echoed the specific blocking finding instead of a misleading download. The current-view and outline endpoints showing operation='replace' with the modified_leaf back-pointer to m1-0-1-cover-letter is precisely the relationship an HC reviewer replays, so I could see the lifecycle was correct, not just trust it.

Very clear at almost every step. When export got blocked I wasn't confused — the 409 literally said 'validation_not_passed' and named CA-REP-0001, telling me to file a Dossier ID Request through REP and Rename before filing, which is exactly the terminology my seniors use. The validator report spelling out what it checks vs does NOT check (and that it's not the official eValidator) removed the guesswork I'd normally have to ask about. The replace-vs-second-copy behavior on the 1.0 cover letter in 0001 was explained inline, so even as someone still learning eCTD lifecycle I understood what happened.

Very clear almost the whole way. Every action gave me a plain-language confirmation ('turns complete', 'both EN and FR attached'), and the validation report named the actual rule ID (CA-REP-0001) with a sentence telling me what to do, not just a red X. The one thing I'd have paused on as a junior is the Rename step re-keying d4821 to e478210 mid-flow - I trusted that placed content 'carries over unchanged' because it said so, but on my first real file I'd double-check nothing dropped. The lifecycle 'replace' view showing the back-pointer to the old cover letter was clearer than anything in my Word-template workflow.

Very clear at each step — I always knew what state I was in and what the system was telling me. The 409 export block spelled out exactly why ('validation_not_passed'), named the blocking rule CA-REP-0001, and told me the fix (file a REP Dossier ID Request, then Rename). The two-signal validation view — structural PASS beside 'HC eValidator: PASS (user attested external)' — was unambiguous about what the tool checked versus what I attested to myself.

Very clear at nearly every step, which for me is the whole ballgame. The validation report didn't just say "failed" — it gave me CA-REP-0001 with a plain-English message telling me to file a Dossier ID Request through REP and rename before filing, so I knew the exact remedy. When export threw the 409, it named the blocking rule instead of dumping a stack trace or, worse, handing me a bad zip. The one thing I'd want spelled out more is the mapping between the rename step and REP itself — it tells me to file the request but I still have to go do that in the real REP portal, and a first-timer might not realize the tool isn't doing that for them.

Unusually clear because the system spoke in my language: rule IDs (CA-REP-0001), the actual remediation ("File a Dossier ID Request through REP, then Rename"), and a coverage panel that lists what is and isn't checked. The 409 export block didn't just fail — it named the blocking finding, so I knew precisely why and what to do. The only thing I had to read twice was the two-signal validate view (structural PASS beside "HC eValidator: PASS — user attested"), but once I saw the external result never flips the structural flag, it was clear.

Very clear at nearly every step, which is unusual. When export blocked, it didn't just fail — it named the exact rule (CA-REP-0001), told me in plain English it was the placeholder ID, and pointed me to the REP Dossier ID Request then Rename path. The validator's own coverage/not_checked block and the standing disclaimer ('this is NOT Health Canada's eValidator') told me precisely what it does and doesn't claim, which is exactly the honesty I look for. The 0001 replace view showing operation='replace' with the modified_leaf back-pointer to m1-0-1-cover-letter is the lifecycle relationship a HC reviewer replays — I could read it at a glance.

At every step I knew what the system was telling me. The validation report didn't just say "failed" — it gave me the rule ID CA-REP-0001 and a plain sentence: placeholder ID, file a Dossier ID Request through REP, then set the real ID. When export blocked with a 409 it literally listed the blocking finding instead of a fake download. The lifecycle 0001 replace even showed me the back-pointer to the superseded leaf. Nothing was a mystery box.

At every step I knew what state I was in and what was left. The killer moment was the export block: HTTP 409 that told me exactly which rule (CA-REP-0001) was stopping me and that it was the placeholder ID, not some vague "cannot export." When I re-keyed to the real HC ID and re-validated to PASS, then watched export succeed with the 9308-byte zip, the cause-and-effect was unmistakable. The replace-vs-second-copy behavior on the 0001 cover letter was clearly labeled too, so I never wondered if I'd just created a duplicate.

Very clear at every step. Findings came back with real HC-style rule IDs (CA-REP-0001) and an actionable message that told me exactly what to do — file the REP request, then Rename. The 409 export block named the exact blocking finding instead of handing me a bad zip, and the criteria block spelling out what IS and ISN'T checked (structural only, not PDF/A-1 ISO profile, not clinical adequacy, not HC acceptance) is exactly the honesty I need to know where my responsibility starts.

Very clear at every gate. When export failed closed it told me HTTP 409 validation_not_passed and named the exact blocking rule ['CA-REP-0001'] instead of dumping a broken zip — that's how eValidator-literate people expect a tool to behave. The rule IDs map to the CA-<severity>-<block> scheme I already read against, the replace op showed operation='replace' with modified_leaf back-pointing at m1-0-1-cover-letter, and the outline replays exactly what HC's reviewer replays. Nothing was ambiguous about what the system was telling me or what to do next.

Very clear at every gate. The progress counter (6/8, 88%, 100%), the validation report with an actual rule ID (CA-REP-0001) and plain-English remediation, and the 409 export block that named the exact blocking finding instead of just failing — I always knew what the system was telling me and what to do next. The lifecycle view showing operation='replace' with a back-pointer to the superseded 0000 leaf was the clearest supersede UI I've seen; that's normally where I have to email the publisher to ask "did it file as a replace or a duplicate?"

Very clear at almost every step. The placeholder banner, the progress counter, and especially the failures told me exactly what to do: CA-REP-0001 named the placeholder ID and literally said "file a Dossier ID Request through REP, then set the real ID (Rename)." The 409 export block didn't just fail, it echoed the blocking rule ID. My one clarity gap: the difference between the tool's structural check and the real HC eValidator — they label it honestly, but I'd want that spelled out for my execs so nobody assumes it's the official validator.

Very clear at almost every step. When export got refused I got a real 409 with the exact blocking rule ID (CA-REP-0001) and a plain-language fix ("file a Dossier ID Request through REP, then Rename"), not a vague error. The validator even told me what it does NOT check — PDF/A profile, hyperlink resolution, HC screening — which is exactly the kind of honesty that stops me over-trusting a green checkmark.

Very clear at every step — the progress counter (0/8 up to 100%) and the complete flags meant I always knew where I stood. The validation report was the standout: real rule IDs like CA-REP-0001 with a plain-language message, plus an explicit checked/not-checked list so I knew it wasn't claiming to judge my scientific content. The 409 export block spelled out the exact blocking finding instead of just failing, and after the Rename the re-validate flipped to PASSED — I could follow the whole chain without guessing.

Very clear at each step. The validation report told me exactly what was wrong with a real rule ID (CA-REP-0001) and plain English — placeholder ID, go get the real one via REP, then Rename — not some cryptic code. When export got blocked it said "validation_not_passed" and listed the same finding rather than handing me a bad download, and after I set the real Dossier ID e478210 it flipped to PASSED and the zip actually came out. The replace op even showed me the back-pointer to the old leaf, which is exactly what a reviewer replays.

Very clear, more than most software I touch. When the export got blocked it didn't just error out, it told me exactly why with rule CA-REP-0001 in plain words: I'm still on a placeholder ID and must file a REP Dossier ID Request, then Rename before filing. The validation report even spelled out what it does and does NOT check, and the outline showed the replace pointing right back at the old cover letter leaf, which is the exact relationship a reviewer replays.

Very clear at every step. The 0% -> 100% module counter, the actual validation report with a real rule ID (CA-REP-0001) and a message telling me exactly to file a REP Dossier ID Request then Rename, and the 409 showing the precise blocking finding rather than a broken download — that is how I think. The replace-op view pointing back at the superseded 0000 leaf (modified_leaf) is exactly the relationship an HC reviewer replays, so I knew the lifecycle was correct.

Very clear at every step. The 0/8 progress counter, the placeholder banner, and the validation report with an actual rule ID (CA-REP-0001) and a plain-language fix ("file a Dossier ID Request through REP, then Rename") told me exactly what to do. The 409 export block named the blocking finding instead of silently failing, and the 0001 outline literally showed operation='replace' with modified_leaf pointing back to the 0000 cover letter — that is the lifecycle relationship a reviewer replays, spelled out for me.

Very clear at almost every step. The checklist labels use the actual HC section numbers (1.0, 1.2.1, 1.2.3, 1.3.1), the validation report gave me a real rule ID (CA-REP-0001) with a plain-English fix ("File a Dossier ID Request through REP, then set the real ID"), and the 409 export block spelled out exactly which finding was stopping me. The one thing I had to read twice was the distinction between the structural check passing and the external eValidator attestation — but the honesty note actually made that clearer, not murkier.

Very clear at every step. The progress counter (0/8 up to 100%) told me where I stood, the validation report named the exact rule CA-REP-0001 in plain language, and the 409 export block spelled out the blocking finding instead of dumping a broken file on me. I especially appreciated that the replace op in seq 0001 showed the back-pointer to the superseded leaf so I could see the supersede was real, not a duplicate.

This earned more trust than any demo I've seen, precisely because it refuses to overclaim. It fails closed on export, it distinguishes its own structural checker (v1.2, synced to HC v5.3) from the real eValidator and makes ME attach the external PASS rather than pretending it ran it, the rename lands on a Part-11 audit trail, and the e-sign manifest is meaning-bearing and tamper-verifiable (re-checksummed 10 leaves, tampered=false). The lifecycle replace produced exactly the modified_leaf back-pointer a HC reviewer replays. I would trust it to ASSEMBLE and gate a real filing — but per its own disclaimer I'd still run eValidator and my own QC before transmit, which is correct.

This earned real trust, and the reason is the honesty. It fails closed — no package emits unless validation genuinely passes — and it never overclaims: the validator explicitly says "This is NOT Health Canada's eValidator," lists what it does and does NOT check (no PDF/A-1 ISO profile, no scientific adequacy, no HC acceptance), and the external PASS is labeled "user_attested_external" and stored as my evidence, never as a tool self-claim of parity. That distinction is what separates a tool I'd stake a client filing on from a toy. The Part-11 e-sign with a meaning, reason, immutable manifest and a working tamper-verify is the audit backbone my QA would demand.

This earned real trust, and the honesty is why. It fails closed on export, it re-ran after my fix and genuinely flipped to PASS rather than just clearing a flag, and critically it never pretends to BE eValidator — the disclaimer explicitly lists what's checked vs not and labels the eValidator result as user-attested-external. That distinction matters enormously to me; a tool that claimed HC-parity would be an instant red flag. The Part-11 e-sign with tamper-verify (re-computing checksums against the live package) is the kind of control our QA would actually accept.

This earned real trust because it fails closed and doesn't overclaim. Watching it refuse to export on the placeholder ID, then pass and emit a 9308-byte zip stamped X-Export-Validation=passed only after I fixed it, is the behavior I want — it won't let me transmit garbage. Critically, it is honest about scope: the validator explicitly says "This is NOT Health Canada's official eValidator," lists what it does and does not check, and stored my eValidator PASS as "user_attested_external" rather than pretending it ran it — that honesty is what makes me trust the rest. The Part-11 e-sign with meaning/reason/signer and a verifiable tamper check (verified=true, tampered=false against re-computed leaf checksums) is the audit backbone we're actually accountable for.

This is where it earned real trust. It didn't just claim things passed — it blocked my export closed on a placeholder ID and refused to hand me a misleading download, then genuinely flipped to PASSED only after I set the real HC ID. The 21 CFR Part 11 e-sign with a tamper-verify that re-checksummed all 10 leaves, plus the honesty that the eValidator PASS is 'user-attested external' and NOT the tool claiming parity, is exactly the kind of no-overclaiming behavior that makes me comfortable. I'd still run the real HC eValidator myself before transmitting — which the tool itself tells me to do — but yes, I'd rely on it to get me to a clean, signed, lifecycle-correct package.

This is what won me over. It refused to export while validation failed (the 409 block) instead of handing me a zip that would bounce at Health Canada - that fail-closed behavior is exactly the mistake I'm terrified of making. And it's honest: it says in plain text this is a structural check, NOT HC's official eValidator, and lists what it does and doesn't check. When I attached my real eValidator PASS it labeled it 'user-attested external' and never pretended the tool itself validated it. That honesty makes me trust it MORE, not less. I'd still run the real eValidator myself before transmitting, which is exactly what it tells me to do.

This is what earned my trust: it fails closed. It refused to hand me a downloadable package while a blocker was open instead of giving me a misleading zip — that's the behavior I want from a system I sign my name behind. The rule IDs map to HC's v5.3 criteria scheme, the e-sign produced a tamper-evident manifest that I re-verified (verified=true, tampered=false over 10 checksummed leaves), the rename and reason landed on a Part-11 audit trail, and the 0001 replace carried a proper back-pointer to the superseded leaf. What clinched it more than any feature: the tool is honest about its limits — it plainly says it is NOT Health Canada's eValidator and records my external result as MY attestation, never claiming parity. A tool that tells me what it does not check is one I can actually rely on.

This earned real trust because it fails closed — it refused to emit a package while validation was red and only produced the 9308-byte zip after the blocker genuinely cleared, stamped X-Export-Validation=passed. What matters even more to me is the honesty: the validator explicitly says "this is NOT Health Canada's official eValidator," lists what it does and does not check (no PDF/A-1 ISO profile, no clinical adequacy), and the eValidator PASS is stored as user-attested external, never a tool self-claim. That's the kind of scoping I need to defend in an audit. The Part-11 side — signer, meaning, reason, immutable manifest under a hash, plus a verify that re-checksums the leaves and returns tampered=False — is exactly what I'd look for, though I'd still want to confirm the audit trail and signing are backed by a validated, access-controlled system before I'd sign for real.

This earned more trust than any prep tool I've used, and specifically because of what it refuses to claim. The disclaimer is exactly right — "Structural and technical checks only. This is NOT Health Canada's eValidator" — and the eValidator attestation is honestly labeled user_attested_external, so the tool never launders my own validation into a tool self-claim. The fail-closed export (won't emit a package while CA-REP-0001 is open) is the behavior I'd demand; it's the opposite of the tools that hand you a clean-looking zip over a broken sequence. I'd still run LORENZ eValidator myself before transmitting — as the tool itself tells me to — but I'd rely on this to get to a clean, lifecycle-correct sequence.

More than I trusted anything at first glance in twelve years of screening. The fail-closed export is the single most important behavior — it refused to hand me a transmissible zip while a blocking finding stood, which is how you prevent a botched sequence reaching HC. And critically, it does NOT overclaim: it maps to the v5.3 rule scheme but explicitly says it is not eValidator, records my external eValidator PASS as 'user_attested_external' with a disclaimer, and never lets that attestation flip the structural pass flag. The Part-11 signing with a tamper-verify that re-hashes the live leaves is real, not theater. I'd rely on it to ASSEMBLE and pre-check — but, as it tells me itself, I'd still run LORENZ eValidator on the exported package before transmitting, which is correct.
